title: Coldcard seed-entropy flaw: $116M–$130M+ swept from wallets with device-generated seeds
summary: A firmware bug shipped in March 2021 (v4.0.1) made Coldcard devices generate seeds from a weak software PRNG instead of the hardware RNG, cutting effective entropy to ~40 bits (Mk2/Mk3) or ~72 bits (Mk4/Mk5/Q). Starting July 30, 2026, attackers brute-forced and swept wallets at scale: ~1,816 BTC / ~$116M from 5,200+ addresses per TRM Labs as of Aug 5; aggregate reporting reached 2,000+ BTC and $130M+ by Aug 10, and Coinkite itself declines to estimate total losses. Updating firmware does NOT fix an existing seed — affected users must generate a new seed on patched firmware and move funds now.

impact.lossNative: ~1,816 BTC (TRM Labs, as of Aug 5 — the verified floor); 2,000+ BTC and $130M+ reported as of Aug 10; Coinkite declines to estimate

timeline.event: Firmware v4.0.1 ships with libngu migration; a #ifndef preprocessor bug silently compiles in MicroPython's Yasmarang software PRNG for seed generation instead of the hardware RNG.
First theft wave: ~594 BTC swept in ~25 minutes (initial sweep tracked at 1,082.65 BTC / ~$70.2M from 1,196 addresses in 41 minutes). Coinkite publishes security advisory the same day.
Coinkite releases emergency patched firmware (Mk2/Mk3: 4.2.0; Mk4/Mk5: 5.6.0; Q: 1.5.0Q). Patch prevents new weak seeds only — existing seeds remain vulnerable.
Advisory updated; four theft waves documented over four days, transaction-construction differences suggest multiple attackers.
Secondary phishing wave: fake 'hardware audit' emails impersonating Coldcard push ScreenConnect remote-access malware. See related incident.
Coinkite declines to estimate total customer losses, saying a post-mortem is in progress rather than speculating on the extent of the theft.
Aggregate tracking passes 2,000 BTC in stolen funds ('the Coldcard exploit has logged more than 2,000 BTC in stolen funds' — Bitcoin.com editor's note).

affected: Seeds GENERATED ON-DEVICE with: Mk2/Mk3 firmware 4.0.1–4.1.9 (~40 bits effective entropy)
Mk4/Mk5 firmware before 5.6.0, Edge before 6.6.0X (~72 bits)
Coldcard Q firmware before 1.5.0Q, Edge before 6.6.0QX
notAffected: Seeds generated with 50+ dice rolls (dice mode bypasses the device RNG entirely)
Seeds imported from elsewhere (the bug is in generation, not storage/signing)
Funds behind a strong, unique BIP-39 passphrase (Coinkite still recommends migrating)
actions: If an affected Coldcard ever GENERATED your seed: treat it as compromised. Move funds to a new wallet today — do not wait.
Update firmware FIRST, then generate the fresh seed on the patched device (or use dice-roll mode / another device), then sweep funds to the new wallet.
Updating firmware alone does NOT protect an existing seed. The seed itself is weak; only a new seed fixes it.
Prefer dice-roll seed generation going forward — 50+ rolls for 12 words, 99+ for 24. See our entropy guide.

Ignore every email/DM offering a 'hardware audit', 'seed check', or 'migration help'. Coinkite will never ask for your seed. Type coinkite.com manually; never click sponsored search results for firmware.

claims.claim: Root cause: MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG set to 0 but guarded with #ifndef (checks existence, not value), so the software PRNG fallback compiled in silently.

The buggy libngu commit was authored under the pseudonymous GitHub account 'Switch'. Media reports have linked that account to a Coinkite principal; we do not name an individual on unconfirmed sourcing — the object of record is the commit and its account.
claims.attribution: Media/social reports; not confirmed by Coinkite

claims.claim: Developer James O'Beirne states he warned Coinkite of exactly this class of defect in May 2025; Coinkite has not responded publicly to that account.
claims.attribution: James O'Beirne (public statements); Coinkite has not commented

claims.claim: No attribution of the thefts; funds mostly pooled with minimal laundering observed as of Aug 5, 2026.

corrections.note: Loss figures restated as an as-of-dated range. Our Aug 8 headline read '~$116M+' sourced to TRM Labs (as of Aug 5). That figure remains the verified floor (~1,816 BTC / 5,200+ addresses), but aggregate reporting has since risen: 2,000+ BTC logged as of Aug 10 (Bitcoin.com) and $130M+ (TechCrunch, Decrypt). Coinkite declines to estimate total losses (Bloomberg, Aug 6). Headline and summary updated to reflect the range; the exact total remains unresolved while thefts are ongoing.
